chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil ibn Darraj, from Yunus ibn 'Abyan and Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

We said: 'May we be sacrificed for you, is it disliked that a man should write in his ring other than his own name and the name of his father?' He said: 'In my ring is written: Allah is the Creator of all things; and in the ring of my father Muhammad ibn Ali (peace be upon him), and he was the best of the Muhammads I saw with my own eyes, is written: The Honour is for Allah; and in the ring of Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) is written: The Praise is for Allah, the Exalted, the Magnificent; and in the ring of al-Hasan and al-Husayn (peace be upon him) is written: Allah is Sufficient for me; and in the ring of Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) is written: Allah is the King.'

key_terms.اللَّهُ خَالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ: Allah is the Creator of all things
key_terms.الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ: The Praise is for Allah, the Exalted, the Magnificent

ai.seo_question: What names can be inscribed on a ring according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi not only permits inscribing names other than one's own and father's on a ring but also provides a historical lineage of epigraphic practices among the Ahl al-Bayt, linking the Prophet Muhammad, the Imams, and Ali ibn Abi Talib. The inscriptions cited—such as 'Al-Wahid' (The One), 'Al-Aziz' (The Mighty), and 'Hasbunallah' (Allah is sufficient for us)—serve as tangible expressions of tawhid and divine attributes, reinforcing the Shia scholarly view that such inscriptions are acts of dhikr rather than mere identification. This practice underscores the continuity of spiritual authority and the emphasis on invoking God's names as a means of seeking protection and closeness to the Divine.
